clue.text: Ingredient for baking, for example, good with milk

parts.note: coffee or tea served with milk is called white

explanation.surface: A recipe note: a baking ingredient, say, made better with a dash of milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with milk' is one piece: white coffee is coffee with milk.
explanation.definitionFit: The albumen of an egg is used in meringues and many cakes, so it is a common baking component.

clue.text: Get ready for hectic chase round Pole

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the pole letter, holding it inside
something hectic is frantic and disordered, so the letters of chase are jumbled

parts.note: N, the North Pole, is one of the two poles

explanation.surface: A frantic pursuit around the North Pole, before which one must get prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hectic' rearranges CHASE to ECASH, and 'round' puts N inside it after the E. 'ready' is slang for cash, so 'Get ready' means turn into cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready money is cash, and to convert a cheque or bond into cash is to get your money out of it.

clue.text: Like 1 ac having good line and first-class trains

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here with the figure as the letter I
RY, short for railway, stands for trains

explanation.surface: Something resembling another entry, with fine qualities and top-quality railway services.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 ac' is 1 across, the white of an egg. A1 (first-class) is entered as AI, using I for the figure one, a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Glair is egg white used as a glaze, so something glairy is slimy and viscous like that albumen.

clue.text: When charges are dropped, pleasing members of the bar

definitions.meaning: a time when drinks prices in a pub are cut for a while
read cryptically, a period of contentment for those drinking at the bar, or lawyers if the bar is the legal profession

explanation.surface: A legal story: the time charges are withdrawn pleases barristers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as courtroom talk, with 'charges' as accusations and 'the bar' as barristers; both are really about pub prices and drinkers.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub's discount period lowers drinks prices, so cheaper charges and cheerful drinkers both describe it.

clue.text: Not portraying the legs of Rugby player

definitions.meaning: a portrait in that format shows the sitter down to the hips or knees, stopping short of the legs
in rugby union, the back positions between the half-backs and the full-back are called this

explanation.surface: A painter of rugby players who leaves out their legs.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby union, the four players between the half-backs and the full-back (the centres and wings) are named for this fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Portraits cut off partway down the body are described by the fraction shown, and rugby names back positions by the same fraction.

clue.text: Dismissal of amateur cricket side

parts.note: lay means non-professional, as in a lay preacher
the off side is one half of a cricket field, opposite the leg side

explanation.surface: An amateur cricket team getting dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the field divides into the off side and the leg (or on) side, split by the line of the batter's stance.
explanation.definitionFit: When staff are dismissed because there is no work for them, that is a redundancy notice.

clue.text: The French in abundance eager over love

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: agog means keenly expectant
love is zero in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: French people, in great numbers, keen on romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a French phrase meaning 'in abundance', so 'The French' tells you the language rather than naming people.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is borrowed from French, where it means plenty or galore.

clue.text: Instructing to leave border in Germany

indicators.note: the clue asks a letter to depart from the word border; the B goes, being the letter on its edge

parts.note: taken as written before the cut
G is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: Telling someone to go off across the frontier into Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to leave' takes B, the letter on the word's edge, from BORDER. G is Germany's international vehicle code.
explanation.definitionFit: To order someone is to tell them what to do, so the present participle means telling or commanding.

clue.text: Provided illumination, like a match at night

definitions.meaning: lit up by floods of light, past tense
an evening football or cricket match is played under powerful lamps

explanation.surface: Lights switched on, as for an evening fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' suggests a thing struck to make fire, but it is a sports fixture played under lamps.
explanation.definitionFit: Powerful lamps lighting a stadium for an evening game give exactly this past participle sense.

clue.text: Drink found in many picnic baskets

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, standing for many
hampers are wicker baskets packed for picnics

explanation.surface: A beverage often packed in hampers for a picnic.
explanation.walkthrough: C, a hundred in Roman numerals, often stands for 'many'. The answer is British slang for champagne.
explanation.definitionFit: This is British informal slang for champagne, a sparkling wine.

clue.text: Bad luck in criminal circles

parts.note: a hood is a gangster or hoodlum
two circles look like the letters O and O

explanation.surface: Misfortune among the gangland underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: A jinx or curse bringing misfortune is called by this voodoo-derived word.

clue.text: Collect computer equipment for the little beast

parts.note: to harvest is to gather a crop
a mouse is a hand-held pointing device for a computer

explanation.surface: Gathering up computer kit for a small animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny rodent of cornfields that weaves nests among wheat stalks is a little beast.

clue.text: Certainly showing no end of petulance

definitions.text: Certainly showing no end of petulance

indicators.note: showing none of a letter means that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: surely means certainly

indicators.note: the last letter of petulance is chosen

explanation.surface: Someone sure of themselves who never stops sulking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of' picks E from petulance, and 'showing no' removes it from SURELY. The whole clue also hints at a sullen temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bad-tempered and rude displays the irritability the clue describes.

clue.text: Displaying smitten demeanour?

indicators.note: smitten means struck hard, so the letters of demeanour are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone whose manner shows they have fallen for someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smitten' is both the anagram signal on DEMEANOUR and part of the picture of a lovestruck manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in love has a lovestruck air, which is exactly what the clue describes.

clue.text: Classic way of coping

parts.note: a Latin phrase (Classic meaning from the classical languages) for a working arrangement that lets people get along

explanation.surface: A tried and trusted method of getting by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic' looks like 'timeless' but signals Latin, the classical language.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin phrase literally means a manner of living, used for a practical arrangement that lets rivals get along.

clue.text: An evil's involved in this

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters of an evil's and in are entangled

parts.note: the apostrophe is ignored and the S counts as a letter here

explanation.surface: Something wicked lies at the heart of this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges AN EVIL'S to VENIALS, with the S counted as a letter; 'in' follows unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: In Catholic teaching a pardonable wrongdoing is a minor transgression, but some wickedness is still part of it.

clue.text: King full of 9? Drag up nothing in the press

indicators.note: the reversed drag word and the zero are placed inside the press word

parts.note: a jam is a crush or press of people

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a bore is a drag, something tedious
nothing is zero, shown as the letter O

explanation.surface: A king brimming with fizz, pushed into the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns BORE to EROB, and with O it goes into JAM. '9' is 9 across, champagne; the answer is both a king of Israel and a large champagne bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A biblical ruler of Israel gave his name to an outsize wine bottle holding several standard bottles of champagne.

clue.text: Dangerous, mount from Northern town

definitions.meaning: an active volcano in Washington State that erupted catastrophically in 1980
a town in Merseyside, in the north of England, known for glassmaking and rugby league

explanation.surface: A treacherous mountain climb starting from a town in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: The same name belongs to a volcano in the USA and a town in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The volcano and the Merseyside town share this saint's name.

clue.text: Forcibly break in? That's resourceful

parts.note: to break in is to go in, or enter
prising means forcing something open with a lever

explanation.surface: A burglar breaking in by force, praised for ingenuity.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer says to go in while levering something open: a forced entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone full of initiative and bold schemes is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Poet we spotted in lounge

indicators.note: the clue says 'we' was seen inside, so those letters go within the lounge word

parts.note: to loll is to lounge lazily

explanation.surface: We saw a poet relaxing in the sitting room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lounge' looks like a room but is the verb, LOLL. Robert Lowell and James Russell Lowell are both American poets.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Lowell was a major American confessional writer of verse.

clue.text: One leader of Persians embraced by another in island

indicators.note: the letter is held inside the second leader's name

parts.note: Cyrus the Great was another leader of the Persians, founder of their empire

indicators.note: the first letter of Persians is taken

explanation.surface: Two Persian rulers in a hug on a Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One leader' is P, the first letter of Persians; 'another' (leader of Persians) is CYRUS, and P goes inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean.

clue.text: Knock for six bowling, with control

parts.note: in cricket, an over is a set of six balls bowled
the helm is the steering, so control

explanation.surface: A cricket over hit for a six, the bowler keeping a tight grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock for six' is a British idiom from cricket meaning to stun or devastate; a six is the maximum hit, over the boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: To be knocked for six is to be utterly overcome or floored, as when emotion swamps someone.

clue.text: Military hero in upward surge by English

indicators.note: in a down clue, upward means read from bottom to top

parts.note: a flow is a surge of water

explanation.surface: A soldier rising on a swell of English patriotism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upward' reverses the surge word to WOLF. James Wolfe was the British general killed winning Quebec in 1759.
explanation.definitionFit: General James Wolfe won the Battle of Quebec in 1759, dying in victory, and became a national hero.

clue.text: Distress exemplified in — The Hunting of the Snark?

definitions.meaning: Lewis Carroll subtitled his nonsense poem 'An ... in Eight Fits', calling the whole work one of these

explanation.surface: Suffering illustrated by Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Carroll called his poem 'An Agony in Eight Fits', the fits being its cantos; the question mark marks the poem as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense pain or anguish is distress, and Carroll used the word for his poem as a whole.

clue.text: Playwright — one I'll put in with minimal revision

explanation.surface: A dramatist says he will add something with only light editing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with minimal revision' says only the apostrophe moves, to just after the O, and the space closes. Eugene O'Neill was the American playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill wrote dramas such as Long Day's Journey into Night and won the Nobel Prize.

clue.text: Rear animal in herd that puts American on wrong track

definitions.text: that puts American on wrong track
definitions.note: read as a noun: something that misleads, in American usage

parts.note: bum is British slang for the backside
a steer is a castrated bullock, one of a herd of cattle

explanation.surface: A cow at the back of the herd leads an American cowboy astray.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stands for 'a thing that puts an American on the wrong track': the phrase is US slang for bad advice.
explanation.definitionFit: This is American slang for misleading information or bad advice that sends someone the wrong way.

clue.text: What's needed for snow-covered motorway, given 25?

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI
a sled is what you need to travel over snow

explanation.surface: Asking what kit you need on a snowbound motorway, after a bad tip.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is a British motorway, and MI stands for it. '25' is 25 across, bad advice; to be given that is to be led astray.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone handed bad advice has been steered wrong, led astray or deceived.

clue.text: Artist's only composition framed by Russians

definitions.note: the definition reads 'artist is', the 's a link

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go inside, as a picture sits in a frame

parts.note: Reds were Russian communists

indicators.note: a composition is an arrangement, so the letters of only are rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter's lone work hung in a frame by Russians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges ONLY to YNOL. Reds is a standard name for Russian communists; Sir Joshua Reynolds was an English portrait painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Joshua Reynolds was the leading 18th-century English portrait painter and first president of the Royal Academy.
